Murder, manslaughter, rape and other listed sex offenses and crimes against children cannot be expunged, and no expungement is available while a person must register as an offender. Arrests that did not lead to conviction can be expunged by petition under a separate statute, K.S.A. 22-2410. Kansas has no automatic expungement process.
errors_in_old: Waiting periods are wrong: misdemeanors are 3 years (not 3-5), except DUI; felonies are 3 years (lower-level) or 5 years (serious), not 5-10. Ten years applies only to a second or later DUI.
'No subsequent convictions during the waiting period' is inaccurate: the statute requires no felony conviction in the past two years and no pending felony proceeding.
Omits arrest/non-conviction expungement (K.S.A. 22-2410) and the list of offenses that can never be expunged.
uncertain: CCRC says the second-DUI wait is 7 or 10 years depending on offense date; the statute summary I read says 10 years with a date carve-out. Summary uses 10.
2026 amendments (HB 2323, SB 430) appear limited to insurance-licensing disclosure and recodification; I did not read SB 430 in full.
K.S.A. 22-2410 details were confirmed only through CCRC, not the statute text.

MI.summary: Michigan calls the remedy setting aside a conviction; official state guidance treats "set aside", "expungement" and "Clean Slate" as the same thing. Under Clean Slate laws passed in 2020, a person can apply to the court to set aside up to three felonies and an unlimited number of misdemeanors. Waiting periods are three years for most misdemeanors, five years for one felony or a serious misdemeanor, and seven years for more than one felony. A first drunk-driving offense without injury can be set aside after five years. Michigan State Police also run an automatic process, now in operation, with no application: misdemeanors after seven years (up to four if punishable by 93 days or more) and up to two felonies after ten years. Excluded are life-sentence felonies, most criminal sexual conduct, repeat drunk driving and human trafficking; assaultive crimes are limited. Arrest records without conviction are handled separately.
errors_in_old: Largely accurate but lacks specifics: waiting periods are 3, 5 or 7 years by application; automatic set-aside covers misdemeanors after 7 years and up to 2 felonies after 10 years.
'Certain non-violent offenses' understates the automatic exclusions, which also cover serious misdemeanors, crimes of dishonesty, offenses punishable by 10+ years and others (per CCRC).
Does not mention limits within the three-felony rule (no more than two assaultive crimes; only one felony punishable by 10+ years) or excluded offenses.
uncertain: Start date of the automatic process (April 11, 2023) appeared only in search snippets of a Michigan AG press release I could not open; summary says only that it is in operation.
Full list of offenses excluded from the automatic process (CCRC lists more exclusions than the AG page; statute MCL 780.621g not read).
Whether the 5-year first-offense OWI wait applies exactly as stated (AG page and CCRC agree; statute not read).

ND.summary: North Dakota's remedy is sealing of the criminal record, created by a 2019 law (N.D.C.C. chapter 12-60.1). A person may petition the court to seal a misdemeanor after at least three years, or a felony after at least five years, without a new conviction; a conviction pardoned by the governor may also be sealed. The court decides case by case; prison and probation terms must be complete and restitution paid. Violent felonies cannot be sealed while the person is barred from possessing firearms, and offenses requiring sex offender registration are excluded. Under a 2025 law, when all charges in a case are dismissed or end in acquittal on or after August 1, 2025, the court closes the record automatically after 61 days; older cases can be closed by petition with no fee. A first marijuana possession offense of one ounce or less can be sealed under a separate provision.
errors_in_old: 'Reduction to infraction' is not the name of North Dakota's sealing process and I found no such sealing remedy; the remedy is a petition to seal under N.D.C.C. ch. 12-60.1 (2019).
Waiting periods stated as '3-5 years for most offenses' are imprecise: 3 years without a new conviction for misdemeanors, 5 years for felonies.
Outdated on non-convictions: since August 1, 2025 dismissed/acquitted cases are closed automatically after 61 days (HB 1166, 2025).
Omits exclusions (violent felonies during the firearm-ban period; sex-offender-registration offenses).
uncertain: Marijuana sealing provision (N.D.C.C. 19-03.1-23(9)) and the two-year condition were confirmed only via CCRC.
A separate DUI-record sealing statute (N.D.C.C. 39-08-01.6) exists per the court's forms list, but I did not open it; left out.
'Closed' non-conviction records remain visible to courts and criminal justice agencies; exact practical effect on background checks not verified.

NY.summary: New York mainly uses sealing: records still exist but are hidden from the public and most employers. Cases that end in the person's favor, such as dismissals and acquittals, are sealed automatically, as are most non-criminal violations. Under the Clean Slate Act, signed in 2023 and in effect since November 2024, most convictions are sealed automatically: misdemeanors three years after sentencing or release, and felonies eight years after release, if the person has no pending charges and is no longer on probation or parole. Sex offenses and most Class A felonies are excluded. The court system has until November 2027 to finish sealing eligible records. Separately, a person can apply to a court to seal up to two convictions, only one a felony, after ten years; violent felonies, Class A felonies and sex offenses are excluded. Laws passed in 2019 and 2021 automatically expunged many marijuana convictions.
errors_in_old: Outdated: omits the Clean Slate Act (signed 2023, effective November 2024), which automatically seals most misdemeanors after 3 years and most felonies after 8 years.
The 10-year sealing by application (CPL 160.59) is limited to two convictions, only one a felony - not stated.
Marijuana convictions were automatically vacated and expunged (2019 law and 2021 MRTA), not merely sealed; so New York does use 'expungement' for marijuana.
Omits automatic sealing of dismissals/acquittals (CPL 160.50).
uncertain: Exact effective date (November 16, 2024) and deadline (November 16, 2027) come from CCRC ('one year after enactment', 'until November 2027') and search snippets of the nycourts.gov page, which blocked direct access.
Current progress of the court system's Clean Slate sealing as of November 2026 - whether eligible records have already been sealed - not verified.
Class A felony exclusion: the statute excepts Class A drug (Article 220) offenses; CCRC words it as Class A felonies subject to a life sentence.

SC.summary: South Carolina uses the term expungement, but only specific categories qualify. Charges that were dismissed or ended in a not-guilty finding can be expunged at no cost; in magistrate and municipal courts this happens automatically. Convictions eligible by application include: minor offenses carrying up to 30 days in jail or a $1,000 fine, three years after conviction with no other conviction (five years for third-degree domestic violence); a first offense under the Youthful Offender Act, five years after the sentence is completed; first-offense simple drug possession after three years; and first-offense possession with intent to distribute after twenty years. Completing pretrial intervention can also lead to expungement. Most categories can be used only once. Driving offenses are excluded, and there is no general expungement for felonies or violent crimes. Applications for convictions go through the circuit solicitor's office.
errors_in_old: Broadly accurate but vague: gives no waiting periods (3 years for minor offenses and simple drug possession, 5 years for domestic violence 3rd degree and Youthful Offender Act, 20 years for possession with intent to distribute).
'Certain first-time offenses' is partly outdated: a 2018 law (H.3209) removed the first-offense requirement for minor summary-court convictions (still once-only).
'Expanded eligibility in recent years' is undated: main expansion was 2018; smaller changes in 2023 and 2024.
Does not mention that relief is generally available only once, or that driving offenses are excluded.
uncertain: Fee amounts ($250 solicitor fee, $25 SLED, $35 clerk) come from CCRC/secondary sources; left out of summary.
Other narrow categories (fraudulent check first offense, failure to stop, alcohol education program, human trafficking survivors) confirmed via CCRC only; not detailed in summary.
Exact timing of the automatic summary-court expungement and its exceptions (objection for pending charges) simplified.

VT.summary: Vermont changed its system in 2025. Act 60, in effect since July 1, 2025, moved from expungement and sealing to sealing in most cases and expanded the list of qualifying crimes. A person may petition to seal most misdemeanors three years after completing the sentence, qualifying felonies after seven years, and a misdemeanor DUI after ten years; restitution and surcharges must be paid. Qualifying felonies are limited to certain burglaries, designated property offenses, certain drug offenses and pardoned convictions. Violent "listed" crimes and offenses requiring sex offender registration do not qualify. Expungement remains for convictions based on conduct that is no longer a crime. Charges that were dismissed or ended in acquittal are generally sealed by the court within 60 days unless a party objects. Sealed records stay available to criminal justice agencies. A 2020 law automatically expunged older small-amount marijuana possession convictions.
errors_in_old: Outdated: since July 1, 2025 (Act 60 / S.12) the main remedy is sealing, not expungement; expungement remains mainly for conduct that is no longer a crime.
Waiting periods are wrong: now 3 years (misdemeanors), 7 years (qualifying felonies), 10 years (misdemeanor DUI) - not '5-10 years'.
The '2019' expansion date is unsupported by the sources I opened; CCRC describes expansions in 2018 and 2025.
'Certain felonies' should be specific: only a short list of felonies qualifies (some burglary, property and drug offenses, pardoned convictions).
uncertain: Whether a 2019 act also expanded qualifying crimes (not confirmed).
Exact scope of the 'certain regulated drug offenses' felony category and of excluded misdemeanors (statute read via summary tool only).
Vermont courts' own self-help page (vtcourts.gov/criminal/expungement) returned a server error, so court practice details were not checked.
Special rule for offenses committed at ages 18-21 (petition 30 days after sentence completion, 13 V.S.A. 7609) left out for space.

CO.summary: Colorado calls record clearing "sealing". When a case ends in acquittal, complete dismissal, or a completed diversion or deferred judgment, the court is meant to seal it automatically; if that does not happen, a motion can be filed with no fee. Many convictions can be sealed by motion after a waiting period that runs from one year for petty offenses to five years for the most serious eligible offenses. Under the Clean Slate Act (2022), courts also seal eligible convictions automatically: after four years for civil infractions, seven years for petty offenses and misdemeanors, and ten years for felonies. Automatic sealing began in 2024, and non-drug felonies were added in July 2025. Class 1, 2 and 3 felonies, DUI, crimes of violence, sex offenses, domestic violence and child abuse convictions are generally not eligible. Restitution must be paid before a conviction is sealed by motion.
errors_in_old: Says automatic sealing covers 'certain drug offenses' only: outdated. The Clean Slate Act (SB 22-099, 2022) covers all petition-eligible convictions except Victim Rights Act crimes: civil infractions, petty offenses, misdemeanors, drug felonies and, since July 1, 2025, other eligible felonies.
Does not mention that non-conviction cases (dismissal, acquittal, completed diversion/deferred judgment) are sealed by the court automatically, with a no-fee motion as fallback.

'Specific provisions for marijuana offenses' is vague and partly outdated: the 2017 marijuana-specific petition law was repealed in 2019 and folded into general drug sealing; a 2021 law (HB 21-1090) and a 'conduct no longer prohibited' motion (C.R.S. 24-72-711) now apply.
No waiting periods or exclusions given (not wrong, but incomplete).
uncertain: Petition waiting period for ordinary misdemeanors: the court's January 2026 clinic slides say 2 years for class 2/3 and drug misdemeanors and 3 years for class 1 misdemeanors and class 4-6 felonies; CCRC summarises it as 3 years for misdemeanors. Summary uses only the 1-to-5-year range.

Clean Slate waiting periods (4/7/10 years) were confirmed from CCRC and an unofficial reproduction of C.R.S. 13-3-117, not from an official state page; the Judicial Branch pages confirm the auto-sealing process and lookup tool exist but do not state the periods.
Whether unpaid restitution blocks automatic (as opposed to petition) sealing was not confirmed.
No published figures found on how many felony records have actually been sealed since July 2025.

HI.summary: Hawaii uses the term "expungement", and it is handled by the state's Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center. It mainly covers arrests or charges that did not lead to a conviction. It is not available where bail was forfeited or the person left the state to avoid prosecution. After a deferred acceptance of a guilty or no contest plea, there is a one-year wait after discharge and dismissal. Convictions can be expunged only in a few categories and only by court order: first-time drug offenders, first-time property offenders, and drivers under 21 with a measurable amount of alcohol. There is no general expungement for other misdemeanor or felony convictions, and a pardon does not expunge a record. Since July 1, 2025, court records are sealed automatically once an expungement order is issued. Hawaii has no automatic clean slate law; a task force created in 2024 is studying one.
errors_in_old: 'Expungement by gubernatorial pardon' is wrong: a pardon in Hawaii does not expunge or seal the record; both the conviction and the pardon remain on the record.
Omits the conviction categories that can be expunged by court order (first-time drug offender, first-time property offender, under-21 alcohol driving offense).

Deferred acceptance (DAGP/DANC) is not limited to 'first-time non-violent drug offenders'; it is a general deferral for people without a prior felony charged with eligible offenses, and expungement is available one year after discharge.
Omits the 2023 law (effective July 1, 2025) under which court records are sealed automatically after an expungement order.
uncertain: CCRC reports a 2026 law (HB2279) extending non-conviction expungement to people arrested or charged with a crime but convicted only of a violation; not confirmed on the Attorney General's page, so left out.
Status of the Hawaii County marijuana arrest-record expungement pilot (2024, expanded 2025) could not be confirmed.
Whether the Clean Slate task force's work has led to legislation; none found as of November 2026.
Fees ($35 first time, $50 otherwise) and the 120-day processing time are from the AG page but left out of the summary as details likely to change.

KY.summary: Kentucky uses the term "expungement". Since 2020, cases that end in acquittal or dismissal with prejudice are expunged automatically, with no action needed; traffic cases are excluded. Misdemeanor convictions can be expunged by petition five years after the sentence or probation ends. A 2016 law opened expungement to some Class D felonies, and a 2019 law extended it to most Class D felonies. The wait is five years after completing the sentence, probation or parole. Class D felonies involving DUI, sex offenses, offenses against a child, abuse of public office, or serious injury or death are excluded, and more serious felony classes are not eligible unless pardoned. A petition needs a certificate of eligibility, which costs $40. Felony expungement costs $300 in total: a $50 filing fee plus $250 if granted. Kentucky has no automatic expungement of convictions.
errors_in_old: Outdated: mentions only the 2016 law. A 2019 law (SB 57) extended eligibility to most Class D felonies and cut the felony fee from $500 to $50 filing plus $250 on grant.
Omits the 2020 change making expungement of acquittals and dismissals with prejudice automatic (no petition or fee).
The 2016 date, the five-year wait and the filing-fee/hearing statements are otherwise accurate.
uncertain: Start date of automatic non-conviction expungement: CCRC says cases disposed after March 27, 2020; the Kentucky courts page says dismissed or acquitted on or after July 15, 2020. Summary says only 'since 2020'.

Misdemeanor five-year wait and the rule that it is mandatory with a single conviction and discretionary with several come from CCRC (KRS 431.078); the courts page refers to the statute without restating the period.
Misdemeanor filing fee ($100 per CCRC) not confirmed on an official page.

2026 SB 290 (Automatic Expungement Act) had not become law per the legislature's bill page (last action March 20, 2026). A 2026 act amends KRS 431.073 effective April 30, 2027; it appears only to add one statute to the list of eligible offenses.

MN.summary: Minnesota uses the term "expungement", which means sealing a record, not destroying it. By petition, a judge weighs the benefit to the person against public safety. Dismissed cases and acquittals have no waiting period; completed diversion needs one year. Convictions need a period without a new conviction after the sentence is discharged: two years for misdemeanors, three for gross misdemeanors, and four for felonies on a set list of mostly nonviolent offenses. Felonies outside that list generally cannot be expunged, and neither can offenses that require sex offender registration. The Clean Slate Act (2023) took effect January 1, 2025, and automatically seals non-convictions, most misdemeanors and many listed felonies in state criminal history records; the state reports about two million records sealed by November 2026. A 2023 cannabis law automatically sealed lower-level cannabis records and created a board to review felony cannabis cases.
errors_in_old: Waiting periods are wrong. Current law (Minn. Stat. 609A.02, as amended 2023): 2 years for misdemeanors, 3 years for gross misdemeanors (not 1-5), and 4 years for listed felonies (5 years for certain felonies deemed misdemeanors/gross misdemeanors); there is no 5-10 year felony range.
Does not say that only a set list of felonies is eligible; other felonies cannot be expunged.
Omits the Clean Slate Act (automatic expungement, in effect since January 1, 2025) and the 2023 cannabis expungement provisions.
The balancing-test statement is accurate.
uncertain: Automatic expungement excludes some categories (CCRC lists drug convictions and reduced-level convictions as requiring a petition); the exact exclusions were not confirmed in the statute text.
Whether automatic waiting periods match the petition periods in every category was not checked against Minn. Stat. 609A.015.
The mncourts.gov help page loaded only partially (overview text); petition details were confirmed from the statute instead.
A 2024 law added a 5-year path for felonies deemed gross misdemeanors/misdemeanors that are not on the list; left out of the summary for simplicity.

NE.summary: Nebraska has no general law for sealing or expunging adult convictions. Records of cases that did not end in conviction are removed from the public record automatically: one year after arrest if no charges were filed, two years if charges were not filed because of completed diversion, and right away after an acquittal or dismissal, including dismissal after a deferred judgment or a drug court program. For convictions, the main remedy is a "set-aside". It is open to people sentenced to probation, a fine, community service, or (since 2020) up to one year of incarceration, once the sentence is complete. A set-aside nullifies the conviction and removes civil disabilities, but it does not seal the record, and it is not available to people on the sex offender registry. Sealing of a conviction is available after a pardon (since 2018) and for trafficking victims whose convictions were set aside.
errors_in_old: Broadly accurate, but says non-conviction records 'allow for sealing' without noting this happens automatically under Neb. Rev. Stat. 29-3523 (immediately on dismissal/acquittal; 1 year if no charges; 2 years after diversion).
Omits the set-aside remedy (29-2264), which is the main relief for convictions though it does not seal the record, and the sealing available after a pardon or for trafficking victims.
Mentions juvenile sealing, which is outside the scope of an adult-records summary.
uncertain: A 'Clean Slate Act' bill (LB 215, 2025-2026) was introduced; a committee amendment reportedly removed the clean slate provisions and no source showed it becoming law. Final status not confirmed on the Legislature's bill page.
The Nebraska Judicial Branch self-help page on set-asides returned 404 (site moved to nebraskajudicial.gov), so official confirmation is from statute text only.
29-2264 was last amended in 2024 (LB 20); CCRC describes LB 20 as a voting-rights law, and the set-aside eligibility rules above match the current statute text.

OH.summary: Ohio has two remedies: "sealing", which hides a record from most public view, and "expungement", which destroys it. A 2023 law (SB 288) rewrote the rules and added expungement of convictions. Sealing can be requested six months after final discharge for minor misdemeanors, one year for misdemeanors and fourth- and fifth-degree felonies, and three years for third-degree felonies (no more than two). Expungement can be requested after six months for minor misdemeanors, one year for misdemeanors, and for felonies ten years after they become eligible for sealing. Final discharge includes paying restitution. First- and second-degree felonies, felony offenses of violence, sex offenses requiring registration, offenses with victims under 13, and most traffic and DUI convictions are excluded. Dismissals, acquittals and no-bills can also be sealed. Everything requires an application to the court; Ohio has no automatic clearing for adults.
errors_in_old: 'First-time offenders' is wrong: the first-offender limit ended in 2012, and since 2023 eligibility depends on the offense, with no cap on the number of misdemeanors or fourth/fifth-degree felonies.
'3-year waiting period for felonies' is only right for third-degree felonies; fourth- and fifth-degree felonies have a 1-year wait. Minor misdemeanors have a 6-month wait.
'Expanded eligibility in 2018' is outdated; the governing overhaul is SB 288, effective 2023 (the statute was last amended effective September 30, 2025).
'Ohio uses the term sealing rather than expungement' is now wrong: since 2023 Ohio offers both sealing and true expungement of convictions.
uncertain: Whether the 2025 amendment (HB 96, effective September 30, 2025) changed anything beyond the points checked; the waiting periods and exclusions in the summary are from the current statute text.
Exact scope of the traffic exclusion and of the domestic violence rules (some misdemeanor DV convictions can be sealed but not expunged, others are excluded) is simplified.
Non-conviction rules (R.C. 2953.33; 2-year wait for no-bills) are from CCRC only.

SD.summary: In South Dakota, "expungement" means sealing a record, and it applies mainly to cases without a conviction. A person may ask the court for expungement one year after an arrest if no charges were filed, one year after the prosecutor dismisses the entire case, or at any time after an acquittal. A 2022 change allows an earlier request after a dismissal on a showing of compelling necessity. There is no general expungement for convictions. Instead, petty offenses, municipal ordinance violations and Class 2 misdemeanors are automatically removed from the public record after five years if all court-ordered conditions are met and there are no new convictions; a 2021 law shortened this from ten years. Records are also sealed after a successfully completed suspended imposition of sentence, which is open to people with no prior convictions for most offenses, and after completed diversion (since 2018).
errors_in_old: Wrong: South Dakota does not allow expungement of 'certain misdemeanors and minor felonies after waiting periods ranging from 5-10 years'. Court expungement (SDCL 23A-3-27) covers only arrests without charges, dismissals and acquittals.

The only time-based conviction relief is automatic removal from the public record of petty offenses, municipal violations and Class 2 misdemeanors after 5 years (10 years before 2021); felonies and Class 1 misdemeanors are not covered.

'Requires that all court costs and restitution be paid' is not a stated requirement for expungement; the payment condition appears for automatic removal (court-ordered conditions satisfied) and for pardons.
Omits the one-year waiting periods for non-conviction expungement and sealing after a suspended imposition of sentence.
uncertain: Suspended imposition of sentence details (eligibility, mandatory sealing under SDCL 23A-27-17) and diversion expungement are from CCRC only.
Sealing after a pardon (SDCL 24-14-11) exists per CCRC but was not confirmed on an official page and is left out of the summary.
Filing fee ($72 per CCRC) not confirmed on the court's page.

WA.summary: Washington's main remedy is "vacating" a conviction. A court sets the conviction aside, and the person may then state they were not convicted of that crime, although the court file is not sealed. Most misdemeanors can be vacated three years after the sentence, with five years for domestic violence cases. Class C felonies need five years and class B felonies ten years after release or sentencing, with no new convictions. Violent offenses and crimes against persons, most sex offenses and felony DUI cannot be vacated; a 2019 law opened second- and third-degree assault and second-degree robbery in some cases. The same 2019 law lets adult misdemeanor marijuana convictions be vacated with no waiting period. After the 2021 State v. Blake decision, drug possession convictions from on or before February 25, 2021 can be vacated. Vacating requires a court request; there is no automatic process for adult convictions.
errors_in_old: Mostly accurate. 'The effect is similar' to expungement overstates it: a vacated conviction is not sealed or destroyed, the court record stays public with a 'vacated' note, and the conviction can still be used in later prosecutions.
'Vacation' is used in the statutes, but the summary omits main exclusions (violent offenses, crimes against persons, most sex offenses, DUI limits).
Omits State v. Blake (2021), under which pre-February 25, 2021 drug possession convictions can be vacated, and non-conviction record deletion.
Marijuana expansion was a specific 2019 law for misdemeanor marijuana convictions at age 21 or older, with no waiting period.
uncertain: Whether any class A felony can be vacated: RCW 9.94A.640 sets waiting periods only for class B and C and bars violent offenses; CCRC is unclear, so class A is not mentioned.

Non-conviction records: CCRC says deletion can be requested from police/State Patrol files 2 years after a favorable disposition or 3 years with no disposition (RCW 10.97.060), with exceptions; not confirmed on an official page and left out.

Whether misdemeanor vacating still requires all court debt to be paid: the statute text refers to completing the sentence including financial obligations; a 2024 change adjusted when the 3-year clock starts.
Misdemeanor DUI can be vacated only after 10 years with no later alcohol/drug violation; simplified out of the summary.

RCW 9.94A.640 was amended in 2025 (c 169, a bill mainly about prison riot offenses); the detail of that change was not reviewed. A 2026 state Supreme Court case (State v. Abrams) on the statute was noted but its holding was not read.
In some counties Blake convictions are vacated on the court's or clerk's initiative without a request.
